name: Mephibosheth
charge: Answering the king, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am; and let him take all
summary: Lame on both feet from the day his nurse dropped him fleeing the news of Gilboa, the last of Saul's line was fetched from Lodebar and given all the land of his grandfather and a place at the king's table continually. When David fled from Absalom his servant slandered him and took the property. When David returned, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven since the day the king departed, and when the land was divided said, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace.
offense: Mephibosheth was five when the news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths caused his nurse to flee with him. He fell in her haste and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). Years later he was summoned from Lodebar to the king who now ruled in his grandfather's place. He came with reverence and fear, but David's purpose was kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1-7). His standing rested upon the covenant between his father and David, not his ability to serve in battle or strengthen the king politically. He received the kindness humbly (2 Samuel 9:8). The promise had reached a member of the former royal house who could offer little power in return. David's care made remembrance of Jonathan a continuing work rather than a passing expression of grief. During Absalom's rebellion Ziba accused Mephibosheth of remaining in Jerusalem to recover Saul's kingdom. When David returned, Mephibosheth came with his neglected feet, beard, and clothes bearing the marks of mourning. He explained that Ziba had deceived and slandered him (2 Samuel 16:1-4; 19:24-28). His answer to the king's order to divide the land was that Ziba could have it all, since David had returned safely (2 Samuel 19:29-30). His joy in the king's preservation stood above the disputed estate.
judgment: David restored Saul's land and appointed Ziba's household to cultivate it, while Mephibosheth ate continually at the king's table as one of his sons (2 Samuel 9:9-13). Provision included both the inheritance's produce and an honoured place in the household. His disability did not exclude him from the kindness pledged to his father. When the Gibeonites required seven of Saul's house, David spared Jonathan's son because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). The broken covenant that brought judgment upon Saul's house was met by a kept covenant preserving Mephibosheth. The king did not allow the pressure of one obligation to make him forget another.
